summary: Sirach 4 begins with urgent commands not to delay help for the poor, the hungry, the wronged, the fatherless, and widows. The chapter then describes Wisdom as a woman who blesses those who seek her, tests them through discipline, and forsakes the one who goes astray. It ends with counsel about shame, truthful speech, courage before the mighty, restraint at home, and open-handed repayment.
whyItMatters: This chapter shows how Sirach joins care for vulnerable people with disciplined pursuit of Wisdom. It also warns that wisdom is not only knowing what is right, but speaking and acting rightly under pressure.

context.author: Yeshua (Jesus) son of Eleazar son of Sira, a Jerusalem teacher and scribe; the Greek translation was made later by his unnamed grandson.
context.audience: Students seeking disciplined wisdom in Jerusalem, and later Greek-reading Jews in Egypt or the wider diaspora.
context.date: The Hebrew work was composed in the early second century BC, likely around 180–175 BC; the Greek translation followed after the grandson came to Egypt, commonly dated to 132 BC.
context.setting: Jerusalem under Hellenistic rule, with Jewish scribal learning, temple-centered worship, and a Greek-speaking Mediterranean world in the background.
context.literaryForm: Wisdom instruction in compact poetic sayings and direct commands.

outline.heading: Do not refuse the needy
outline.note: The teacher warns against withholding help, delaying aid, turning away from the poor, or provoking those already in distress.

outline.heading: Humility and justice in public life
outline.note: The student is told to respect the assembly, listen to the poor, judge without hesitation, and act protectively toward the fatherless and their mother.

outline.heading: Wisdom blesses those who seek her
outline.note: Wisdom is portrayed as a woman who exalts, gladdens, blesses, and becomes an inheritance for those who love, serve, listen to, and trust her.

outline.heading: Wisdom tests and may forsake
outline.note: Wisdom first leads through crooked ways and discipline, then restores to the straight way; the one who goes astray is abandoned to his fall.

outline.heading: Shame, speech, and truth
outline.note: The teacher distinguishes destructive shame from honorable shame, warns against partiality, urges timely speech, confession, and striving for truth.

outline.heading: Restraint and open hands
outline.note: The final sayings warn against hasty speech, negligence, harshness at home, suspicion, and receiving without repaying.

keyVerses.text: For if he curses you in the bitterness of his soul, he who made him will hear his supplication.
keyVerses.why: This anchors the opening section by saying that the cry of the mistreated poor is heard by their maker.

keyVerses.text: Be as a father to the fatherless, and like a husband to their mother. So you will be as a son of the Most High, and he will love you more than your mother does.
keyVerses.why: This verse gathers the chapter’s concern for vulnerable people into the image of active protection and kin-like responsibility.

keyVerses.text: For at the first she will walk with him in crooked ways, and will bring fear and dread upon him, and torment him with her discipline, until she may trust his soul, and try him by her judgments.
keyVerses.why: This is the chapter’s most difficult description of Wisdom: she forms a person through testing before revealing her benefits.

keyVerses.text: Strive for the truth to death, and the Lord God will fight for you.
keyVerses.why: This verse condenses the closing counsel about truthful speech, courage, and refusal to bend before power.

themes: care for the poor and needy

questions.question: Who is being addressed as “My son”?
questions.answer: The chapter opens as instruction from a teacher to a student. The phrase does not require that the speaker is literally the student’s father; in wisdom teaching, family language often frames education and formation. In this chapter, the student is being trained in conduct toward the poor, speech, truth, and Wisdom.

questions.question: What does the chapter say about the poor and needy?
questions.answer: The chapter tells the student not to deprive, delay, reject, or turn away from people in need. It also says to listen to a poor man and answer him peacefully and humbly. The stress is not only on giving things, but also on attention, dignity, and timely response.

questions.question: What is a “suppliant”?
questions.answer: In this chapter, a suppliant is someone asking for help while in affliction. The command is not to reject such a person or turn away from a poor man. The word belongs to the chapter’s larger warning against ignoring distressed people.

questions.question: Why does verse 6 matter?
questions.answer: Verse 6 says that if a wronged person curses in bitterness, “he who made him” will hear his supplication. The chapter does not encourage cursing; it warns the student that mistreating a needy person is not hidden from God. The vulnerable person’s complaint is presented as something God hears.

questions.question: Does verse 10 require becoming a literal replacement husband or father?
questions.answer: The verse uses family roles to describe protective responsibility toward the fatherless and their mother. Readers differ over how directly to apply the images, but the chapter itself points to care, protection, and advocacy rather than a legal arrangement. The promise that follows connects such care with being loved by the Most High.

questions.question: Why is Wisdom called “her”?
questions.answer: This chapter personifies Wisdom as a woman who exalts, tests, blesses, and teaches those who seek her. Sirach regularly presents Wisdom as a figure, not merely as information. In this chapter, the feminine portrayal helps show Wisdom as an active teacher who forms the student.

questions.question: Why would Wisdom lead someone in “crooked ways” and bring fear and dread?
questions.answer: This is one of the chapter’s harder images. The text says Wisdom first disciplines and tests a person, then returns him to the straight way and reveals her secrets. Interpreters debate whether the “crooked ways” describe Wisdom’s difficult training, the student’s experience of confusion, or a testing path meant to prove trustworthiness; the chapter does not spell out the mechanism.

questions.question: What kind of shame is good or bad here?
questions.answer: The chapter distinguishes “a shame that brings sin” from “a shame that is glory and grace.” It then gives examples: do not be ashamed of your soul, do not hide wisdom merely to seem fair, do not speak against truth, and do not be ashamed to confess sins. The point is that shame can either silence what should be said or restrain what should not be done.

questions.question: How does the chapter handle power and partiality?
questions.answer: The student is told not to show partiality and not to revere any man to the point of falling. The chapter also warns not to be partial to the mighty and to strive for truth even to death. Its concern is that fear of powerful people can distort judgment, speech, and action.

glossary.def: A person lacking resources or social power; in this chapter, the poor must not be deprived, rejected, ignored, or answered harshly.
Someone who asks urgently for help; verse 4 places this person in affliction.
Children without a father’s protection; the chapter tells the student to act toward them as a father.
Personified as a female teacher who exalts, tests, blesses, and may forsake those who go astray.
Biased treatment that compromises the soul or favors the mighty instead of truth.
